---
title: "Softmax, Sampling, and Temperature"
subtitle: "How a language model turns scores into a choice — and what that choice does and does not tell you"
---

::: {.callout-note}
**Standalone module.** You do not need to have attended the talk to use
this page. It assumes the probability, likelihood, and discrete-choice
background typical of a PhD economics program, and no machine-learning
background.
:::

## 1. The problem being solved

At every position in its output, a language model must turn an unbounded,
open-ended choice — "what word or token comes next?" — into something a
computer can act on. Two requirements have to be met simultaneously:

- the model needs a **complete probability distribution** over every
  possible next token, not just a single best guess, because a single
  guess cannot express how confident the model is, or represent the fact
  that several continuations may be almost equally plausible;
- that distribution has to be built from whatever internal scores the
  network happens to produce — real numbers of arbitrary sign and scale,
  with no built-in guarantee that they are nonnegative or sum to one.

**Softmax is the fixed function that solves exactly this problem.** It
takes any vector of real-valued scores and returns a valid probability
distribution — every entry nonnegative, all entries summing to one — while
preserving the ranking the scores implied. Everything else in this module
is about what that function looks like, what it shares with a tool
economists already use, and where that resemblance stops.

## 2. A small next-token example

Consider a language model partway through the sentence:

> "Given the traffic data, the agency decided to \_\_\_ the bridge."

A real vocabulary has on the order of $10^5$ possible next tokens. To keep
the arithmetic visible, restrict attention to five plausible candidates:

`repair`, `monitor`, `replace`, `close`, `ignore`

The model's job at this position is to assign a probability to each of
these five words (and, in the background, to every other token in the
vocabulary) that reflects how plausible a continuation it would be, given
everything in the context so far.

## 3. Logits

The last layer of the network does not output probabilities directly. It
outputs one real number per vocabulary entry — a **logit**, conventionally
written $z_i$ for candidate $i$. Logits can be positive, negative, large,
or small; nothing about them individually is a probability, and nothing
requires the full set to sum to any particular value.

| Token | Logit $z_i$ |
|---|---|
| repair  |  2.0 |
| monitor |  1.0 |
| replace |  0.5 |
| close   | −0.5 |
| ignore  | −3.0 |

These five numbers are the model's raw, unnormalized signal that `repair`
is a strong candidate and `ignore` is a poor one — but they are not yet a
distribution.

## 4. The softmax equation

Softmax turns a vector of logits $z = (z_1, \ldots, z_V)$ into a
probability distribution over $V$ items:

$$
p_i = \frac{\exp(z_i / T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V} \exp(z_j / T)}
$$

For now, set the temperature $T = 1$ (temperature is the subject of
§7). Two properties are worth internalizing immediately:

- **every $p_i > 0$.** Even the least likely token gets some probability
  mass; softmax never rules a token out entirely — this is exactly why a
  model can occasionally produce a token that looked implausible.
- **softmax is invariant to a constant shift.** Adding the same constant
  $c$ to every logit leaves every $p_i$ unchanged, because
  $\exp(z_i + c) = \exp(c)\exp(z_i)$, and the $\exp(c)$ factor cancels
  between the numerator and the denominator. Logits have no natural zero
  point; only their *relative* values matter. [S-01]

Applying this to the table in §3 (still at $T=1$) gives
$p \approx (0.60, 0.22, 0.13, 0.05, 0.004)$ for
(`repair`, `monitor`, `replace`, `close`, `ignore`) — nonnegative, summing
to one, and ranked exactly as the logits were.

## 5. The connection to multinomial logit

If this equation looks familiar, it should. **Softmax uses the same
probability mapping as multinomial or conditional logit models**: given a
vector of scores, exponentiate and normalize. [S-02] The role $z_i$ plays
here is the role a linear index $x_i'\beta$ plays in a conditional-logit
choice model.

One genuinely useful piece of discrete-choice intuition survives the
transplant intact. For fixed logits, the ratio of any two probabilities
depends only on those two logits:

$$
\frac{p_i}{p_j} = \exp\!\left(\frac{z_i - z_j}{T}\right)
$$

This is the familiar odds-ratio property associated with independence of
irrelevant alternatives (IIA), and it holds here algebraically, exactly as
it does in a standard conditional-logit model. [S-03]

## 6. The limitations of that analogy

The resemblance is real but narrow, and it is worth being precise about
where it stops.

**The language model as a whole is not a multinomial-logit model.** [S-02]
Only the *final probability mapping* — logits to probabilities — shares
multinomial logit's functional form. Everything upstream of that mapping
(the transformer, its attention layers, its parameters) is what produces
the logits $z_i$ in the first place, and none of that machinery is linear,
low-dimensional, or estimated the way a discrete-choice model's index
function is.

**The algebraic property is not a behavioral one.** For fixed logits,
softmax preserves the algebraic odds-ratio property associated with IIA.
It should not be given a behavioral random-utility, structural, or welfare
interpretation here, because the logits are context-dependent
neural-network outputs rather than estimated utility indices with
structural meaning. [S-03] Concretely:

- $z_i$ is not a linear index in a small set of observed covariates with
  coefficients you could report and interpret; it is the output of a deep
  network with a context-dependent input, and it changes with every word
  added to the prompt.
- There is no independent structural model of "utility" being estimated
  here, and no claim that a change in one alternative's attributes leaves
  the *relative* odds of two unrelated alternatives fixed in any
  economically meaningful sense — only the algebraic identity above holds,
  and only for a fixed vector of logits.
- The "choice set" is not a small number of labeled, economically
  meaningful alternatives; it is on the order of $10^5$ vocabulary entries,
  most of which are not meaningfully in competition with each other for a
  given prompt.

The honest summary: softmax borrows multinomial logit's *arithmetic*, not
its *econometrics*.

## 7. Temperature and sampling

Temperature $T$ rescales every logit — dividing by $T$ — before the
softmax normalization in §4 is applied. It changes how concentrated the
resulting distribution is, without changing which token has the highest
logit.

- **Argmax is deterministic and introduces no sampling variation; sampling
  can produce different continuations from the same probability
  distribution.** These are two different ways of turning a distribution
  into a single output token, and they answer different questions: argmax
  asks "what is most likely?"; sampling asks "draw one token according to
  these probabilities."
- As $T \to 0$, softmax converges to argmax **when there is a unique
  highest logit** — probability mass concentrates entirely on the top
  candidate. (If two or more logits are exactly tied for the maximum, the
  limiting distribution instead splits mass among the tied candidates;
  with real-valued network outputs, exact ties are rare in practice.)
- As $T \to \infty$, the distribution approaches uniform across all
  candidates — every token becomes roughly equally likely regardless of
  its logit.
- Changing $T$ leaves the parameters $\theta$ of the model completely
  untouched. The same trained model, given the same prompt, can produce
  different continuations on different runs purely because of how its
  output distribution is *sampled* — not because anything about the model
  changed.

## 8. The interactive

The laboratory below uses the same five logits from §3. Move the sliders,
change the temperature, and compare a single draw against 100 or 1,000
draws. The empirical frequencies (red markers) should track the
theoretical probabilities (blue bars) more and more closely as the number
of draws grows — the same law-of-large-numbers behavior that governs any
repeated random draw from a fixed distribution.

## 9. A common misconception

**It is tempting to think that lowering the temperature — making the model
more "confident," more deterministic — makes its answers more truthful.
It does not.**

The training objective rewards plausible continuation rather than
independent verification of truth. The parameters encode statistical
regularities rather than a directly queryable source record. Without
grounding or external checks, a plausible continuation can therefore be
unsupported or false.

Sampling affects *variability*, not truthfulness, and is not the root
cause of unsupported claims. **Deterministic decoding — $T \to 0$, always
taking the argmax — can also produce a confident, fluent, and false
answer.** Nothing about §7's temperature mechanics touches whether a
continuation is grounded in fact; temperature only controls how
concentrated the distribution is over continuations the model considers
plausible. [S-08]

## 10. Check your understanding

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>If you add the same constant $c$ to every logit, how does the
probability distribution change?</summary>
It does not change. Softmax is invariant to a constant shift applied to
every logit (§4): the factor $\exp(c)$ introduced by the shift appears in
every term of both the numerator and the denominator and cancels exactly.
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>As $T \to 0$ with a unique highest logit, what does the
distribution converge to?</summary>
A point mass on the single highest-logit token — the distribution
converges to argmax (§7).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Why shouldn't you call $z_i$ "the utility of token $i$," the way
you might call $x_i'\beta$ a utility index in a discrete-choice model?</summary>
Because $z_i$ is the output of a deep, context-dependent neural network,
not a linear index in a small set of observed covariates with estimable,
interpretable coefficients. Treating it as a utility index imports a
behavioral or welfare interpretation the model was never estimated to
support (§6).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>True or false: lowering the temperature to make the model's
answer more "confident" also makes that answer more likely to be
true.</summary>
False. Temperature controls how concentrated the output distribution is
over continuations the model already considers plausible; it says nothing
about whether the training objective ever checked those continuations
against truth. Deterministic decoding can produce confident, unsupported
answers just as readily as sampling can (§9).
</details>
:::

## 11. Continue learning

- **3Blue1Brown, *Transformers, the tech behind LLMs*** (video; ~5 min for
  the relevant section, starting at 22:22, "Softmax with temperature";
  full video is part of a longer series). Introductory/visual level. Best
  explanation available of *why* softmax needs a normalizing sum and how
  temperature reshapes it, with a direct animated derivation. Included
  because it is the clearest visual counterpart to §4 and §7 above.
  Limitation: does not discuss the multinomial-logit connection or its
  limits (§5–§6 above) — that framing is this module's own contribution.
  <https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/gpt>

- **Andrej Karpathy, *Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT*** (video; the
  segment beginning at 26:01, "inference," runs roughly 5 minutes; the
  full video is 3.5 hours). Introductory level, plain language. Shows
  sampling in the context of a full autoregressive generation loop, which
  this module deliberately does not build (see §7's cross-reference to a
  later module on generation). Limitation: no equations — purely
  conceptual; pair it with §4–§7 above for the mathematics.
  <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=1561s>
